questions.question: A periodic-review single-item inventory model assumes discrete random demand, a fixed lead time, backlogging of unmet demand, and that unsold items carry over to the next period. Which product violates one of these assumptions?
options: Tinned soup whose daily demand is random and varies from day to day.
Screws whose supplier always delivers exactly two weeks after an order.
Fresh fish that must be thrown away at the end of each day if unsold.
Books for which customers wait when the shop is out and collect later.

questions.question: In a periodic-review inventory system with lead time $l\ge1$, $Q_j$ is the order placed at the start of period $j$, $D_k$ the demand in period $k$, and a prime marks end-of-period values. In which order do the events of period $k$ take place?
options: $Q_{k-l}$ arrives, $Q_k$ is placed using $P'_{k-1}$, then $D_k$ is met from $I_k$.
$D_k$ is met first, then $Q_k$ is placed using $P'_k$, and $Q_{k-l}$ arrives at the end of period $k$.
$Q_k$ is placed using the level $I_k$, then $D_k$ occurs, and only then does $Q_{k-l}$ arrive.
$Q_{k-l}$ arrives and is added to $P_k$, then $D_k$ is met, then $Q_k$ is placed using $P'_k$.

questions.question: An inventory system can be seen as a queue viewed from the other side. In a single-item system with backlogging, what is waiting, and for what, while the inventory level is positive?
options: Customers wait for items, and the level counts the waiting demand.
Items on the shelf wait for demand, and the level counts them.
Orders in transit wait to arrive, and the level counts them.
Empty shelf space waits for deliveries, and the level counts free space.

questions.question: In a periodic-review single-item inventory system with backlogging, a demand finds no stock on the shelf. What happens to this demand in the model?
options: It is served at once from the units ordered but still in transit to the shop.
It is lost, so it is subtracted from neither the level nor the position.
It is kept, but served only after all new demand of later periods is met.
It is kept as a negative level and served first from the next deliveries.

questions.question: In a single-item inventory system with discrete random demand, why are the parameters of an $(s,S)$ policy chosen by simulating each candidate pair rather than from a formula such as the EOQ?
options: The EOQ with mean demand gives the best pair, and simulation only checks it.
Its average cost has no closed form, so each pair is evaluated on a demand path.
One simulated demand list gives the exact long-run expected cost of a pair.
Demand is continuous, so the recursions cannot be worked out by hand at all.

questions.question: A single-item system with backlogging has lead time $l=0$ and uses a base-stock policy $Q_k=S-P'_{k-1}$ with $S=6$. Period $k-1$ ends with $I'_{k-1}=P'_{k-1}=-2$ and nothing on order; period $k$ has demand $D_k=5$. What is the end-of-period level $I'_k$?

An $(s,S)$ policy will be chosen by a grid search that simulates every candidate pair on one demand list. The reorder level ranges over $s\in\{1,\dots,5\}$, the order-up-to level over $S\in\{3,\dots,7\}$, and a pair is valid only if $s<S$. How many pairs are simulated?

A five-period simulation of a single-item system records the orders placed at the starts of periods $2$ to $6$ as $Q_2=0$, $Q_3=6$, $Q_4=0$, $Q_5=5$, $Q_6=7$, with $Q_1=0$. An order cost $K=10$ is paid per order placed. What is the average order cost per period over periods $1$ to $5$?

A make-to-order production queue corresponds to a base-stock policy, the $(s,S)$ policy with $s=S-1$, here with $s=-1$; it orders $Q_k=S-P'_{k-1}$. A period ends with inventory position $P'_{k-1}=-2$. What are $S$ and the order $Q_k$?
options: $S=1$ and $Q_k=3$
$S=0$ and $Q_k=2$
$S=0$ and $Q_k=0$

questions.question: A single-item system with lost sales starts period $k$ with inventory level $I_k=4$ and position $P_k=12$ (8 units on order). The demand is $D_k=7$, and only demand that can be met from stock is accepted. What is the end-of-period position $P'_k$?
Candidate pairs $(s,S)$ of an inventory policy are compared by simulating each one over $n$ periods. Why should every candidate be run on one and the same demand list?
options: Then every candidate places its orders in exactly the same periods.
Then the simulated average equals the exact expected cost of each pair.
Then the estimated costs no longer depend on the horizon length $n$.
Then cost differences come from the parameters, not from different demand.

questions.question: A shop loses demand that finds no stock, and is simulated with the lost-sales recursion from a non-negative start level. Its manager keeps the backlogging cost $Kq+h\overline{I^+}+b\overline{I^-}$, where $\overline{I^-}$ averages the start-of-period backlogs. What must change?
options: Nothing, since $b\overline{I^-}$ now measures the lost units instead of backlog.
The holding term $h\overline{I^+}$ must go, since lost units leave no stock behind.
$\overline{I^-}$ stays $0$, so a lost-demand cost must replace $b\overline{I^-}$.
The order term $Kq$ must go, since a lost-sales shop places fewer orders.

questions.question: A single-item system with backlogging has lead time $l=0$, so an order placed at the start of period $k$ arrives at once. Why can a backlog still occur in period $k$?
options: $Q_k$ is fixed from $P'_{k-1}$ before $D_k$ is known, so $D_k$ may exceed $I_k$.
With $l=0$ an order placed at the start of period $k$ is usable only at its end.
Backlog from earlier periods is never cleared by later orders in this model.
With $l=0$ position and level differ, and the policy reacts to the position.

questions.question: A single-item system with backlogging charges backlog cost $b=4$ per unit of backlog present at the start of a period. Over periods $1$ to $4$ the start levels are $I_k=4,1,-1,3$ and the end levels $I'_k=1,-2,-3,-1$. What is the average backlog cost per period?

An $(s,S)$ policy with $s=2$, $S=7$ orders $Q_{k+1}=S-P'_k$ at the start of period $k+1$ whenever the end position $P'_k\le s$. The lead time is $l=1$, backlog is allowed, $I_1=P_1=7$ with nothing on order, and $D_1=5$, $D_2=5$, $D_3=6$. What is $I_4$?

A single-item system with lead time $l=2$ starts with nothing on order. The orders placed at the starts of periods $1$ to $5$ are $Q_1=0$, $Q_2=0$, $Q_3=10$, $Q_4=6$, $Q_5=3$. By how much does the position $P_5$ exceed the level $I_5$ at the start of period $5$, after ordering?
The single-item model assumes a fixed lead time $l$. Suppose instead that each order's lead time is random. Which of the two recursions $I_k=I'_{k-1}+Q_{k-l}$ and $P_k=P'_{k-1}+Q_k$ breaks, and why?
options: Only the position recursion, since the position must wait until the order arrives.
Only the level one, since orders may overtake and the arrival is no longer $Q_{k-l}$.
Both, since with random lead times demand is no longer independent across periods.
Neither, since lead time only matters for lost sales and not for backlogging.

questions.question: A simulated policy shows several periods ending with $I'_k<0$, yet its average backlog cost $b\overline{I^-}$, with $\overline{I^-}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=1}^{n}I_k^-$ from start-of-period levels, is $0$. How is this possible?
options: Each backlog was cleared by an arrival at the next period's start, before costs.
A zero backlog cost means no period ended with backlog; the record must be wrong.
Backlog cost is charged only for lost units, and a backlogging system has none.
This happens only with lead time $l=0$, where the order and the demand coincide.

questions.question: A make-to-order queue is run as a base-stock policy with $S=0$ and lead time $l=1$: at the start of period $k$ it orders $Q_k=-P'_{k-1}$, started from $I_1=P_1=0$ with nothing on order. Demands are $D_1,\dots,D_5=3,5,2,6,1$. What is the backlog $I_5^-$ shown by the start-of-period level $I_5$, that is, the number of jobs waiting at the start of period $5$?

Demand is constant, $D_k=3$ per period; an $(s,S)=(0,12)$ policy with $l=0$ orders $12-P'_{k-1}$ when $P'_{k-1}\le0$. An order of $12$ arrives at the start of period $5$. With $K=24$ per order and $h=1$ per unit on hand at each period start, what is the average cost per period over periods $5$ to $8$?
